source_title: Traverse Performance Characterization for the Mars Science Laboratory Rover (Heverly et al.; Journal of Field Robotics 30(6), 2013)
vehicle: DTM (MSL Dynamic Test Model, 437 kg, 128 percent of flight Mars weight, six wheel rocker bogie)
grousers: chevron grousers at 15 deg spacing, 7.5 mm radial height (Sec 3)
soil: Marsyard cohesionless sand, well sorted, some subsurface moisture detected
preparation: artificial sand slopes in a U shaped retaining wall, flat to 25 deg, track 5 m by 9 m
gravity_g: 1 (Earth test; vehicle mass chosen for Mars weight)
comparability_note: Points are bin medians of all marker pixels found by colour masking in 1 deg slope bins (pixel weighted, so runs with more plotted samples weigh more); x_unc and y_unc combine the reading error with half the interquartile range of the masked pixels in the bin. Slip = 1 minus traverse distance over commanded distance, in percent, from 10 s windows at 1 Hz (GPS) or 2 Hz (motion capture), Eq. 2 to 4; slope is measured rover pitch. Constructed slope of well sorted sand at 1 g with some subsurface moisture (paper notes packing between grousers), so not a natural dune; vehicles embedded near 17 deg (Sec 6.3). Negative slip values are measurement noise per the paper. load_per_wheel_N derived here from Table I Earth weight 4287 N divided by 6 wheels (equal share assumed).

grousers: 14 grousers, 20 mm long (flight wheel: 15 mm, skeletonised)
soil: Toyoura sand, loose (about 25 percent relative density)
preparation: loose packing checked with a hand vane against calibrated bulk density samples
comparability_note: Seed pixels read by eye for the red + experiment markers, refined automatically to the column of the vertical error bar and the midpoint of that bar (error bars are symmetric about the mean); error bar half lengths are not transcribed. Forced slip on level loose Toyoura sand at wheel speed 0.2 rad/s, Earth gravity, nominal 24.5 N per wheel for the 10 kg Rashid-1 rover. Toyoura sand is a uniform laboratory quartz sand (0.15 to 0.3 mm), close in grain size to fine dune sand but better sorted.

source_title: Analysis of Angle of Attack for Efficient Slope Ascent by Rovers (H. Inotsume, Master's thesis, 2016)
figure_or_table: Figure 3.9 (slip at angle of attack about 90 deg) with Table 3.2 actual slopes; Sec 3.4.1 text
vehicle: Scarab rover set to 400 kg, four rigid wheels, active suspension disabled (Table 3.1)
soil: GRC-1 lunar regolith simulant (manufactured), loosened
preparation: SLOPE tilt bed 6 m by 4.5 m, 0.23 m deep, soil loosened and levelled before each test; slope measured by stereo plane fit
comparability_note: x values are the actual slopes printed in Table 3.2 for the 90 deg runs; y digitised from markers (means over the run, error bars 1 SD not transcribed). Slip ratio s = 1 minus vx over vref (Eq. 3.1). GRC-1 is a manufactured lunar simulant with a wide grading, not dune sand; 400 kg rover with large smooth wheels at 1 g. Soil properties from Table 2.1 (loosened). load_per_wheel_N derived here as 400 kg times 9.81 divided by 4 wheels. The last point is text, not digitised.

source_title: Analysis of Angle of Attack for Efficient Slope Ascent by Rovers (H. Inotsume, Master's thesis, 2016)
vehicle: El-Dorado-II four wheel rover, 35 kg, steering fixed (Table B.1)
soil: Toyoura standard sand, dry, cohesionless
preparation: sandbox 2 m by 1 m, soil loosened and levelled before each run, box jacked to the slope angle (up to about 20 deg)
comparability_note: Seed pixels read by eye on the 300 dpi raster, refined to the centroid of the series colour within the stated radius; markers are means of three runs, error bars (1 SD, not transcribed) visible on some points. Slip ratio from motion capture and wheel encoders, wheel speed 1.8 rpm. Small 35 kg rover at 1 g on dry Toyoura sand is close in scale to a small dune rover, but Toyoura sand is a uniform laboratory quartz sand and the bed is shallow and freshly loosened. load_per_wheel_N derived here as 35 kg times 9.81 divided by 4 wheels. Unpublished campaign reported only in this thesis appendix.

source_title: Characterization of traverse slippage experienced by Spirit rover on Husband Hill at Gusev crater (Li et al.; JGR Planets 113, E12S35, 2008)
evidence_row: not in evidence.csv (FLD-010 to FLD-012 are Spirit rows from another source)
vehicle: MER Spirit rover (six wheel rocker bogie)
load_per_wheel_N: not reported
soil: Spirit terrain class fine grain, Gusev crater, Mars
preparation: natural terrain, Husband Hill, Gusev crater, sols 154 to 737; terrain class assigned manually from rover images per traverse segment
comparability_note: Points are medians of marker pixels in 2 deg slope bins (pixel weighted, so roughly marker weighted); x_unc and y_unc combine reading error with half the interquartile range in the bin. Each published dot is one short visual odometry segment (mean 0.51 m); absolute values of slope and slip are used for forward and backward drives (para 39), so ascents and descents are pooled and this is not strictly direct ascent. Overlapping dots near zero slip are under counted. Terrain classes assigned manually. Mars gravity 0.38 g, 177 kg rover, basaltic soil.
